title: HERO: A hierarchy-aware analysis pipeline for reducing and refining whole-brain atlas-mapped cellular datasets
summary: Advances in high-throughput mesoscale microscopy and machine learning-based image analysis pipelines have made unbiased whole-brain imaging widely accessible. However, translating the resulting atlas-mapped datasets into biologically meaningful results remains a substantial barrier owing to their sheer magnitude and complex hierarchical organization. Consequently, reporting structure and analysis methods vary widely across studies, undermining rigor and reproducibility. To address this, we developed a user-friendly data reduction workflow, HERO (Hierarchy-aware Expression Region Organization), designed to perform hierarchy-aware selection, refinement, ranking, and visualization of whole-brain cell detection datasets. The workflow is customizable to specific needs, requires minimal coding experience, and outputs transparent, curated results. HERO functions as a seamless plug-in within larger-scale whole-brain cell detection analysis pipelines, providing efficient, unbiased region selection to streamline subsequent statistical analyses and comparative evaluations. Although HERO is developed with mouse cell-detection datasets, it can be applied to any atlas-mapped dataset that contains hierarchical information. Here, we applied the HERO pipeline to example cell detection datasets containing afferent cells from the bed nucleus of the stria terminalis (BST) and the insular cortex (insula). HERO provided top projecting regions consistent with historical tracing studies for the BST (e.g., amygdalar and hypothalamic regions) and the insula (e.g., somatosensory, autonomic, and interoceptive regions). Furthermore, the refinement step of HERO provides additional enriched regions originally obscured in the primary ranked outputs, such as memory- and emotion-associated structures. With HEROs dynamic processing, we were able to identify top-projecting regions consistent with the literature and, additionally, find regions often obscured in these large datasets. In sum, HERO offers a standardized analysis workflow to reduce whole-brain cell-detection datasets, transforming raw regional cell counts into curated results and advancing the effectiveness, interpretability, and accessibility of whole-brain imaging in neuroscience.

title: Neural signatures of glioma progression using implanted neural interfaces
summary: High-grade glioma is an incurable brain cancer with a median survival of approximately 14 months. Over the last 50 years, small improvements in patient outcomes have been overshadowed by significant progress in most other cancers. Yet, emerging research has revealed that neural circuits play an active and central role in driving glioma growth and proliferation, highlighting the nervous system as a promising avenue for both disease monitoring and therapeutic intervention. Here, we present a platform for chronically monitoring tumor progression using neural recordings in freely behaving mice with gliomas. Using this platform across multiple mouse strains and glioma models, we show that neural recordings can accurately track tumor progression in vivo. Cancer progression was consistently associated with elevated gamma-band neural activity in the tumor microenvironment across both adult glioblastoma (GBM) and pediatric diffuse intrinsic pontine glioma (DIPG) cancer models. Interestingly, lower frequency neural activity exhibited distinct, cell-line specific changes over time: GBM models exhibited decreases in low frequency neural activity whereas DIPG models exhibited increases over time. Finally, using machine learning models applied to chronic neural recordings from tumor-bearing mice treated with or without standard-of-care chemotherapy (temozolomide for GBM), we accurately predicted tumor burden as inferred through in vivo bioluminescence imaging. By fitting low-dimensional mathematical models to gamma-band neural trajectories, we could further predict individual tumor growth rates over a 5-week period with high accuracy. These results establish that pathological neural-tumor interactions can be harnessed to monitor glioma progression in vivo. Coupling this monitoring capability with therapeutic electrical stimulation in the same device could open up a new class of implantable, closed-loop neurotechnologies with the potential to transform glioma treatment.

title: From Ligand Binding to Pore Opening in the Mosquito Odorant Receptor AaegOR10
summary: Mosquito olfaction is central to host seeking and other behaviors relevant to vector ecology and disease transmission. Mosquito odorant receptors (ORs) are ligand-gated ion channels, yet how ligand binding is coupled to pore opening remains poorly understood. Here, we combine more than 400 $\mu$s of aggregate molecular dynamics simulations and adaptive sampling with Markov state models (MSMs) and electrophysiological measurements to characterize the gating dynamics of \textit{Aedes aegypti} odorant receptor 10 (AaegOR10). Interaction analysis identifies M288 as a persistent contact between $o$-cresol and S6, connecting the orthosteric pocket to a conformation-dependent hydrophobic network involving I293, F294, and F356 at the S6-S7b interface. The MSMs place the experimentally determined open and closed structures within a multistate conformational landscape and identify a principal intermediate along the dominant gating pathway. A localized S6 kink in this state is associated with weakened S6-S7b coupling and increased flexibility of the pore-lining S7b helix. Ligand binding shifts the conformational equilibrium toward open states and shortens the transition times from the closed state to both the intermediate and open states. We also identify an off-path closed state characterized by a pronounced inward displacement of S6, with phospholipid headgroup insertion observed in some sampled conformations. Mutational analysis and voltage-clamp recordings support the functional relevance of M288, the S6-S7b interface, and the kink-prone S6 region. Together, these results describe a multistate pathway linking ligand recognition to AaegOR10 pore gating.
